prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Before anything could happen, flecks of real gold on her mouth, her eyes more convex than any others, the ground spoke, the barrier of lilacs spoke. What sang in the black tree was entirely gold. Her chair was empty. New absence is a great figure dark as the underskin of fruit. At the center of the earth it surrounds and amplifies the dead whose music never slows down. She came by car. I came by train. We embraced. It was at the foot of a hill steeply crowned with apples and a ruined fortress. Imagination did not make the world. Sweetness is the entire portion. Before anything could happen, happiness, the necessary precondition of the world, spoke and flowered over the hill. When I was in Hell on the ruined palisade, either mystery or loneliness kissed my open eyes. It felt hugely convex, seeing and immediately forgetting. By contrast, what I imagined later was nothing.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker depicts a surreal landscape where the ground, lilacs, and a black tree seem to speak or sing.
- An empty chair and a “new absence” suggest the presence of death or loss at the center of the scene.
- Two people arrive separately, embrace, and meet near a hill crowned with apples and a ruined fortress.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The text explores grief, absence, and happiness through surreal, dreamlike imagery of gold, landscape, reunion, and a ruined hilltop fortress. It suggests that lived feeling and presence exceed imagination, making sweetness and happiness the essential conditions through which the world becomes meaningful.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Before, What, Her

outputs.L1:
Before anything could happen, with flecks of real gold on her mouth and eyes more convex than any others, the ground spoke; the barrier of lilacs spoke. What sang in the black tree was entirely gold. Her chair was empty. New absence is a great figure, dark as the underskin of fruit. At the center of the earth, it surrounds and amplifies the dead, whose music never slows.

She came by car. I came by train. We embraced at the foot of a hill, steeply crowned with apples and a ruined fortress. Imagination did not make the world. Sweetness is the entire portion. Before anything could happen, happiness—the necessary precondition of the world—spoke and flowered over the hill.

When I was in Hell, on the ruined palisade, either mystery or loneliness kissed my open eyes. It felt immensely convex: seeing and immediately forgetting. By contrast, what I imagined later was nothing.
outputs.L2: Before events had any chance to begin, with actual specks of gold on her lips and eyes rounder and more protruding than anyone else’s, the earth began to speak, and so did the wall of lilacs. The song coming from the black tree was pure gold. Her seat stood vacant. A fresh absence becomes an immense shape, as dark as the skin beneath fruit. Deep in the earth’s core, it encloses and magnifies the dead, whose music never loses tempo. She arrived in an automobile. I arrived by rail. We held each other. This happened at the base of a hill, sharply topped with apple trees and the remains of a fortress. The world was not created by imagination. Sweetness is all that is given. Before anything else could occur, happiness—the essential condition that allows the world to exist—spoke and burst into bloom across the hill. When I was in Hell, standing on the broken palisade, either solitude or mystery pressed a kiss onto my open eyes. The sensation was vast and rounded, perceiving and at once erasing what it saw. Compared with that, everything I pictured afterward amounted to nothing.
outputs.L3:
The passage presents a surreal and highly symbolic landscape in which the natural world appears to be alive with language and music. The ground, the lilacs, and even a black tree seem to speak or sing, creating the impression that the scene is not merely being observed but is actively communicating. This gives the landscape a dreamlike intensity, as though nature itself has become a voice for feeling, memory, or revelation.

At the center of this strange setting is an empty chair and what is described as a “new absence.” These details introduce a strong sense of death, loss, or disappearance. The chair suggests someone who should be present but is no longer there, while the phrase “new absence” implies that the loss is recent and still deeply felt. Rather than being a simple background detail, this absence becomes central to the emotional meaning of the scene. The landscape may be full of sound and animation, but it is organized around emptiness.

Into this setting, two people arrive separately. Their separate arrivals suggest distance, isolation, or different paths of experience, yet they eventually come together in an embrace. Their meeting takes place near a hill crowned with apples and a ruined fortress, images that combine fertility and decay, promise and collapse. The apples may suggest abundance, desire, or life, while the ruined fortress points to history, destruction, or the failure of protection. Their embrace therefore occurs in a place where life and loss exist side by side.

The text also draws a clear contrast between imagination and lived experience. Although the landscape is fantastical and seems shaped by dream or vision, the speaker insists that imagination did not create the world. This insistence gives the scene a powerful reality: however surreal it may appear, it is not merely invented. The world exists before and beyond the mind’s ability to imagine it. Experience, especially emotional experience, has a force that imagination alone cannot equal.

Finally, happiness is presented as something essential to existence itself. It is not treated as a decorative or temporary feeling, but as a necessary condition for fully being alive. Yet when the speaker looks back through memory or imagination, that earlier happiness seems diminished, even empty, by comparison with the original lived moment. The later act of remembering cannot recover the fullness of what was once experienced directly. In this way, the passage becomes a meditation on presence and absence, life and loss, and the painful gap between actual happiness and the shadow of it preserved in memory.
outputs.L4:
The text moves through a landscape of grief and absence, shaping loss into a series of dreamlike images. Gold appears not simply as wealth or brightness, but as something strange and symbolic: a substance of memory, longing, and transformation. The world it describes feels suspended between waking and dreaming, where familiar places become charged with emotion and where the visible landscape seems to reveal hidden states of the soul.

At the center of the text is the tension between separation and reunion. Absence is felt deeply, not as an empty space but as a presence of its own, something that alters the meaning of every object and every view. The ruined hilltop fortress becomes an emblem of this condition. It stands above the landscape like a remnant of another time, suggesting both endurance and destruction. Its ruin evokes grief, but also a strange beauty: what has been broken still remains, and what remains continues to speak.

The imagery of landscape widens the emotional field of the text. Hills, distances, light, and ruins are not merely background details; they become ways of thinking about inner experience. The external world reflects the movement of feeling, especially the ache of longing and the fragile hope of return. In this sense, the text treats grief as something that transforms perception. To grieve is to see differently, to find signs of loss and desire in the shape of the world itself.

Yet the text does not remain only in sorrow. It also turns toward happiness, sweetness, and the possibility of renewed presence. Reunion is imagined as something more powerful than fantasy, because real feeling exceeds what the mind can invent. The beloved presence, or the fullness of lived experience, cannot be reduced to an image or a dream. Imagination can gesture toward it, but actual happiness surpasses imagination. It is richer, more immediate, and more necessary.

The text therefore suggests that meaning is not created by thought alone. The world becomes meaningful through feeling, through the sweetness of experience, and through the happiness that allows things to appear fully alive. Happiness is not treated as a simple mood or a temporary pleasure, but as a condition of perception. It is what lets the world shine, what turns landscape into revelation, and what makes presence more real than any imagined substitute.

In the end, the text presents grief and happiness as intimately connected. Absence teaches the value of presence, while sorrow sharpens the desire for sweetness. The ruined fortress, the golden imagery, and the dreamlike landscape all point toward the same insight: that human experience is larger than imagination, and that the deepest truth of the world is reached not through abstraction, but through lived feeling. Sweetness and happiness become the essential conditions by which the world is not only seen, but understood.
outputs.L5:
Before the sun rose, she stood by the window and wondered what the day would bring. Her thoughts moved quietly between memories and hopes, between the things she had lost and the things she still wished to find.

Before everything changed, life had seemed simple. What she wanted had once been clear, but now her heart felt full of questions. Her journey was not easy, yet she knew that every step forward mattered.

What waited ahead, she could not know. But her courage was stronger than her fear, and before long, she began to believe in herself again. Her story was still being written, and this time, she would choose the next chapter.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in the style of a fragmented dream narrative, using images of gold, lilacs, apples, a ruined fortress, trains, cars, absence, happiness, and Hell.
counterfactuals.output:
In the station of my sleep, the trains arrived without engines, dragging long ribbons of gold through the fog.

Nobody stepped down.

The platform smelled of lilacs and burnt sugar. Somewhere, behind the ticket window, a child was laughing with the careful happiness of someone counting knives. I asked for a map and received an apple, red on one side, black on the other, warm as an animal heart.

“Eat it,” said the absence beside me.

But absence had no mouth, no hands, no shadow. Only a coat hanging in the shape of a person. Only a place at the table where the spoon kept moving by itself.

Beyond the tracks stood a ruined fortress, its towers cracked open like old teeth. Vines climbed the stones and bloomed in impossible lilacs, purple as bruises on the sky. Cars circled the walls endlessly, headlights on in daylight, their drivers faceless, their horns singing hymns from Hell.

I climbed the fortress stairs.

At each landing, a different room of my life was burning quietly: a kitchen full of rain, a bed made of railway timetables, a garden where golden apples fell upward into the clouds. In one chamber, happiness sat on a throne of rusted wheels, wearing a crown too heavy for its small bright skull.

It beckoned.

I went closer and saw that its smile was a door.

Behind the door: Hell, but not fire. Hell was a waiting room painted pale yellow, with lilacs in a vase and no water. Hell was the sound of a train departing just as you remember where you meant to go. Hell was an empty passenger seat in every car passing through the city at dusk.

I held the apple to my ear.

Inside it, someone was whispering my name from a great distance, perhaps from the bottom of a well, perhaps from childhood, perhaps from the golden throat of a bird nailed to the sun.

Then the fortress began to move.

Stone by stone, it rolled forward on invisible tracks, gathering speed. The cars followed. The trains followed. The lilacs shook loose their petals and became snow. Absence sat beside me at last, fragrant and terrible, and together we watched the world recede through a window that had never been there before.

I was almost happy.

That was the worst part.

In the dream, I bit the apple.

In the waking, I found gold dust on my tongue.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, lyrical paragraph of experimental fiction that feels like a translation of an avant-garde European poet, with recurring phrases and uncanny imagery.
counterfactuals.output: At the hour when the balconies began to remember their birds, I walked backward through the city of milk-glass, saying, this is not exile, this is not exile, while the tramlines shone like wet nerves under the tongue of evening. In every window a woman with my mother’s hands was sewing black snow into a child’s sleeve; in every fountain a horse lowered its head and drank its own reflection until only the bridle remained. I had been translated poorly from the language of stones, and so my pockets were full of echoes, blue nails, tickets to stations that had never consented to exist. Do not open the cupboard, said the cupboard, and inside it the sea was folding its shirts with bureaucratic tenderness. This is not exile, I said, but the word exile grew little roots in my mouth, grew lamps, grew a corridor where a blind violinist polished the moon with a crust of bread. Above us the angels of rust descended, not singing but counting—one burnt orchard, two porcelain wolves, three brides asleep in the throat of a bell—and the sky, that old accomplice, put on its paper mask. I wanted to ask the dead for directions, yet the dead were busy becoming furniture in the ministry of rain; their drawers opened and shut all night, all night, like eyelids in a fever. Somewhere a dog barked in Latin, somewhere a saint undressed into feathers, somewhere my own name crossed the square carrying a suitcase of thawing mirrors. And still I walked, backward, backward, past the bakeries where ash was braided into bread, past the schools where children learned the alphabet of smoke, past the hospital in which every bed contained a small, obedient forest. This is not exile, said the forest. This is not exile, said the tram. This is not exile, said the black snow falling upward through the lamps, and because I believed them, because I believed everything that had no face, I entered the last doorway and found there, waiting on a chair of salt, the first morning of the world, coughing politely into a handkerchief of flame.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poetic meditation on grief and memory where the landscape speaks, an empty chair signifies absence, and the narrator recalls meeting a woman near a hill with apples and ruins.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk the hill begins to speak.

Not in words, exactly—  
but in the slow grammar of grass,  
in the wind turning over each blade  
as if searching for a name it once knew.  
The stones murmur beneath their moss,  
old teeth of a house the weather has chewed down,  
and the apple trees lean together,  
heavy with their small red lanterns,  
remembering hands.

I came here first with a woman  
whose laughter moved lightly over ruin.  
She stood where the wall had fallen,  
one palm resting on a broken sill,  
as though listening for the vanished rooms  
inside the silence.  
Behind her, apples shone in the branches—  
bright, impossible,  
like promises the earth had forgotten to keep.

She said the hill was older than sorrow.  
She said even grief, given time,  
would become part of the landscape:  
a shadow beneath a tree,  
a path no one admits to making,  
a chair left out in the rain.

Now the chair waits by my window,  
empty as a held breath.  
Its wooden arms are worn smooth  
where hers once rested;  
its seat gathers the evening light  
and gives nothing back.  
Absence has weight—  
not like stone,  
but like snow accumulating  
on a branch until the branch remembers  
how to bend.

I sit beside it and listen.

The valley speaks in lowered tones:  
the river carrying away yesterday’s face,  
the crows stitching black thread through the sky,  
the hill drawing its blanket of mist  
over apples, over ruins, over all  
that cannot be repaired.

And memory, that patient orchard,  
drops one fruit at a time.

Here is her hand lifting an apple.  
Here is the dust on her hem.  
Here is the ruin behind her  
opening its roofless mouth to the weather.  
Here is the light saying stay,  
though nothing stays.

I have learned  
that grief is not the opposite of love.  
It is love kneeling  
in the place where someone has vanished.  
It is the empty chair  
keeping the shape of the body.  
It is the hill, each evening,  
telling the same old story  
to anyone willing to hear:

What is gone is not silent.  
What is lost is not nowhere.  
The earth keeps everything—  
footstep, apple, bone, song—  
and gives it back as wind,  
as blossom,  
as the ache that ripens  
whenever the trees grow full  
and the ruins glow briefly gold  
before night.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surrealist prose poem beginning with “Before anything could happen,” and include the lines “Her chair was empty” and “Imagination did not make the world.”
counterfactuals.output:
Before anything could happen, the clocks removed their faces and laid them like pale lilies on the floor. The room inhaled. A spoon trembled in its saucer, remembering the sea, and the window opened inward onto a field of blue horses sleeping beneath the snow.

Her chair was empty.

Still, the table kept speaking to her in crumbs. It told of a city buried under a loaf of bread, of angels with ink-stained knees, of a moon that had been mistaken for a doorknob and turned until night entered the house.

I waited with my hands full of rain. The walls leaned closer, listening for the first word that would make the ceiling blossom. But no word came. Only the moths, carrying tiny lamps, circled the absence as if it were a saint.

Imagination did not make the world.

It merely found it there, already impossible: the black apple on the plate, the fish swimming through the mirror, the empty chair growing roots into the floorboards, patiently becoming a tree no one would ever sit beneath.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract, dreamlike passage about happiness as the precondition of the world, blending death, music, fruit, gold, and a journey by train to meet someone who arrives by car.
counterfactuals.output:
Happiness was not in the world; it was what the world had to pass through before becoming visible. It lay beneath the day like gold under a thin skin of dust, soft and incorruptible, making even sorrow shine at the edges.

In that country the dead were not gone, only listening. They stood among the orchards with their hands full of pears and dark plums, their faces turned toward a music no one had yet begun to play. When the first notes came, they loosened from the trees like ripe fruit, falling without bruising, entering the grass with a sound almost like laughter.

I took the train at evening. The windows filled with fields, then water, then fields again, all of it trembling in the blue reflection of my own face. Every station seemed abandoned and expectant, as if the world were holding its breath between one happiness and the next. In my pocket I carried a coin, or a sun, or the memory of a sun: something round and golden that warmed my palm whenever I thought of death.

You were coming by car from the other direction. I imagined the headlights moving through the dusk like two white violins, drawing music from the road. I imagined your hands on the wheel, the dashboard glowing with its small constellations, apples rolling on the back seat, a bouquet of yellow flowers opening and closing their eyes.

By the time I arrived, night had ripened. The platform smelled of iron, rain, and oranges. Somewhere a bell rang—not to announce departure or arrival, but to prove that sound itself could be a kind of fruit, split open and sweet. Then your car turned into the station yard, washed in gold from the lamps, and for a moment everything was simple: the train behind me breathing like an animal, the dead singing softly in the trees, the world beginning again because happiness had already agreed to it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
